results.summary: This design implements two leaky integrate-and-fire neurons connected by a synapse with spike-timing-dependent plasticity, using 8-bit fixed-point arithmetic. The first neuron receives an 8-bit input current on ui, the second neuron's state is driven out on uo, and spike outputs plus the 6-bit synapse weight appear on the bidirectional pins. It is tested by applying current patterns and observing spike timing and weight changes, optionally with a logic analyzer or signal generator. The project is notable for putting a small plastic spiking neural network on a single Tiny Tapeout tile.

ttUART is a UART repeater that mirrors received serial data back out on the transmit line. It exposes rx_data_in, rx_data_ready, rx_sample_clk, tx_data_out and tx_data_done pins and can be used like a regular UART. No external hardware is required. The documentation is very brief, giving only the repeater behavior and pin functions.

UltraTiny-CPU is a minimal 8-bit CPU with an accumulator, a B register, a program counter and a 16-byte internal instruction memory. It is programmed through a load mode where ui[7] selects loading, ui[3:0] supplies the address and uio[7:0] supplies the byte, then runs from address 0 with results visible on the accumulator output uo[7:0]. No external hardware is strictly required, though a logic analyzer or LED display can be attached to watch the accumulator. The design is notable for fitting a complete fetch-decode-execute loop and small instruction set into a single tile.

ITS-RISCV is a RISC-V based system that boots by configuring an external SPI flash into XIP mode and executing instructions directly from it. It exposes SPI signals (sclk, cs_n, mosi, miso) and four GPIO pins that can be used for purposes such as bitbanged UART. It is tested with a testbench containing an SPI flash model preloaded with a Verilog hex program, and the project is built and simulated through FuseSoC. The design requires a compatible SPI flash chip and is notable for being a compact RISC-V XIP system derived from PicoSoC.

UW ASIC - Optimized Dino is described as a Dino game compressed into only two tiles. The documentation consists entirely of placeholders, so the actual controls, video output format and testing method are not stated. The pin names are generic and give no further detail about the interface. There is essentially no usable documentation for this project.

This is a silicon implementation of an Enigma I cipher machine with a limited three-wire plugboard and a 52-bit key length. It takes 5-bit data and 3-bit command inputs, returns data on the bidirectional pins with a ready signal, and drives the on-board 7-segment display. No external hardware is needed because it uses the PCB's built-in display. The design is notable for implementing a historical rotor cipher machine in Amaranth on a single tile.

Traffic-light-sequence implements a simple traffic light state sequence from red through red-yellow, green and yellow back to red. Two input pins select the state and three output pins drive the corresponding lights. It is a Wokwi project with no tiles, intended as a basic educational demonstration. The documentation is minimal and does not describe any external hardware beyond the implied LEDs.

This project uses two ring oscillators whose outputs are sampled by a D flip-flop at a 10 kHz clock to produce a pseudo-random bit and its complement on two output pins. It is operated simply by applying power, after which the oscillators are expected to run and the sampled random outputs appear on OUT0 and OUT1. No external hardware is required. The documentation is thin and the design is a Wokwi simulation with no tiles, so no silicon behavior is reported.

Redco is a reconfigurable digitally controlled oscillator built from a five-inverter ring oscillator feeding a flip-flop clock divider. It can be used as a ring oscillator by shorting out0 back to the input, or as a clock divider and DCO selected by three binary control pins, with outputs on out0 and out1. The documentation explains the pin functions and configuration but the project is a Wokwi design with no tiles and no measured silicon results. No external hardware is specified.

Yohan Tiny Tapeout Project is described as a mixed logic gate design intended to control a 7-segment display. The documentation states that the project is a work in progress, that the gates make signals do funky things, and that the testing method is still to be determined. It lists a seven-segment display, input board, output board and switch panel as external hardware. The documentation is too incomplete to describe the actual function or verify the pin behavior.
